old: The supplementary runs under uniform 0.4 separate this reduction into two components: lower error on corrupted labels and increased error on initially correct labels (Appendix I.2). The former exceeds the latter in all 15 dataset–seed runs. Random grouping also lowers Brier scores, but yields much lower classification accuracy, showing that target error and downstream performance capture different aspects of supervision.
new: A further analysis on Cora, CiteSeer, and CoraFull separates the reduction in error on corrupted labels from the increase on initially correct labels (Appendix I.2). Under uniform 0.4 noise, the reduction outweighed the increase in all 15 runs.

old: The representation used for grouping determines which training nodes contribute labels to each target. Table 7 compares the frozen GRACE representation with raw attributes X and two-step propagated attributes A2X on Cora, CiteSeer, and CoraFull under uniform 0.4 noise. The propagated representation uses the original adjacency matrix without added self-loops or adjacency normalization; the resulting node vectors are L2-normalized as in Eq. (3). All three conditions were rerun over five paired seeds using the setup in Appendix I.1; ball counts are reported as ranges across those seeds.
new: The representation determines which nodes are grouped together and hence which labels contribute to each target. Table 7 compares GRACE with raw node attributes X and two-step propagated attributes A2X on Cora, CiteSeer, and CoraFull under uniform 0.4 noise. Propagation uses the original adjacency matrix without added self-loops or adjacency normalization, followed by L2 normalization of the node vectors as in Eq. (3). All three conditions use five paired seeds and the common setup in Appendix I.1. The ball counts show the range across seeds.

old: Under the same construction settings, neither raw attributes nor propagated attributes yield an accepted split in any of the 15 dataset–seed runs. All nodes therefore remain in one granular ball. For each training node, the two representations give the same consensus from all other training nodes, the same soft target, and identical accuracy under the paired training procedure. GRACE produces multiple balls, allowing each target to draw on a smaller local group. The accuracy differences in Table 7 show that the representation affects whether the fixed splitting rule forms useful regions for supervision.
new: With the same splitting parameters, raw X and A2X both produced a single ball in all 15 runs. Each node therefore drew its consensus from all other training nodes rather than a local subset. The identical partitions produced identical soft targets and classification accuracy for each paired seed. GRACE produced multiple balls and higher accuracy on all three datasets. Under the chosen splitting rule, its learned representation therefore enabled more useful local grouping than either of the two simple representations.

old: We also examine pretraining variability using three GRACE seeds, each evaluated with three downstream seeds under uniform 0.4 noise. The adjusted Rand index [74], which measures agreement between partitions, ranges from 0.247 to 0.365 across pretraining seeds, indicating differences in node assignments. After averaging accuracy over the three downstream seeds for each representation, the standard deviation across pretraining seeds is 0.13, 0.45, and 0.60 percentage points on Cora, CiteSeer, and CoraFull, respectively. Mean accuracy exceeds MLP+CE for every pretraining seed. Thus, classification performance remains relatively stable across these runs despite changes in the specific partition.
new: We next varied the GRACE pretraining seed, using three pretrained representations and three downstream seeds for each. The resulting partitions differed: their adjusted Rand index [74], a measure of agreement between partitions, ranged from 0.247 to 0.365. Classification accuracy, however, was relatively stable. After averaging over downstream seeds, its standard deviation across pretraining seeds was 0.13, 0.45, and 0.60 percentage points on Cora, CiteSeer, and CoraFull, respectively. GB-LCSS exceeded MLP+CE for every pretraining seed. Thus, the tested representations yielded different node assignments but similarly effective supervision under uniform 0.4 noise.

old: We varied one parameter at a time on Cora, CiteSeer, and CoraFull under uniform 0.4 noise, using five paired seeds and fixed pretrained representations (Appendix I.1). Increasing Bmax from 64 to 128 changed mean accuracy by 0.00, 0.21, and 1.57 percentage points, respectively. Cora still formed 52–53 balls, whereas CoraFull reached 128 balls and improved on all five seeds. Increasing β from 0.5 to 1 improved CiteSeer by 1.74 points but gave little average benefit on the other two datasets.
new: We varied one parameter at a time on Cora, CiteSeer, and CoraFull under uniform 0.4 noise, keeping the pretrained representations fixed and using five paired seeds (Appendix I.1). Increasing the ball budget Bmax from 64 to 128 changed mean accuracy by 0.00, 0.21, and 1.57 percentage points, respectively. Cora still formed 52–53 balls, whereas CoraFull used all 128 balls and improved on every seed. Increasing the majority-class weight β from 0.5 to 1 improved CiteSeer by 1.74 points, with little change on the other two datasets.

old: The support and split thresholds have clearer failure cases. Raising smin from 2 to 10 reduced the fraction of training nodes receiving consensus correction to 56.53% on Cora and 58.32% on CiteSeer, with accuracy decreases of 7.27 and 5.22 points. Setting δ=0.10 prevented all splits on the three datasets, whereas δ=0.01 produced the same targets as the default 0.05. The effect of nmin differed across datasets. These results show that region resolution and voting coverage both matter; the default values provide a common configuration rather than a dataset-wise optimum.
new: Requiring more votes can leave fewer nodes able to use local consensus. Raising smin from 2 to 10 reduced this coverage to 56.53% on Cora and 58.32% on CiteSeer, while accuracy fell by 7.27 and 5.22 points. The split threshold also mattered: δ=0.10 prevented all splits on the three datasets, whereas δ=0.01 produced the same targets as the default 0.05. Changes to the minimum ball size nmin had mixed effects across datasets. In these tests, the largest losses occurred when a setting prevented local groups from forming or substantially reduced the number of nodes receiving consensus supervision.

old: Unless varied in Section 4.3.4, GB-LCSS uses Bmax=64, nmin=32, δ=0.05, smin=2, and β=0.5 as the default settings. Recursive 2-means uses Euclidean distance, k-means++ initialization [71], and 10 initializations per candidate split, with randomization controlled by the downstream seed. The graph encoder uses the fixed GRACE configurations listed in Appendix F and is frozen after pretraining. The distillation extension uses temperature τ=1. Complete parameters and their sources appear in Appendix F.
new: GB-LCSS uses Bmax=64, nmin=32, δ=0.05, smin=2, and β=0.5 as the default settings. Recursive 2-means uses Euclidean distance, k-means++ initialization [71], and 10 initializations per candidate split, with randomization controlled by the downstream seed. The graph encoder uses the fixed GRACE configurations listed in Appendix F and is frozen after pretraining. The distillation extension uses temperature τ=1. Complete parameters and their sources appear in Appendix F.

old: We evaluated Cora, CiteSeer, and CoraFull under uniform 0.4 training-label noise, with the 20%/10%/70% split, clean validation labels, and seeds 0–4. Each dataset used the same frozen GRACE representation as the main comparisons. The target rule, MLP architecture, optimizer, 200-epoch budget, and validation-based checkpoint selection were unchanged. Each alternative was compared with a default run using the same split, noise realization, and initialization seed.
new: These experiments use Cora, CiteSeer, and CoraFull with uniform 0.4 noise on training labels, a 20%/10%/70% split, clean validation labels, and seeds 0–4. Each dataset retains the frozen GRACE representation used in the main comparisons. Each parameter variant is paired with the default configuration using the same split, noise realization, and initialization seed. The target rule, MLP architecture, optimizer, 200-epoch budget, and validation-based checkpoint selection remain unchanged.

old: For these runs, targets were computed on the CPU and MLP training used an AMD Radeon RX 7700 XT with PyTorch 2.9.1+rocm7.2.1. The sklearn 1.8.0 two-means routine used six CPU threads; PyTorch used four host threads. Table 7 and Table I.1 report this paired rerun. All parameter differences below are measured against its default, not against a result from a different numerical execution path.
new: Targets were computed on the CPU, and the MLP was trained on an AMD Radeon RX 7700 XT using PyTorch 2.9.1+rocm7.2.1. The scikit-learn 1.8.0 implementation of 2-means used six CPU threads; PyTorch used four host threads. The default configuration was rerun with this setup and serves as the reference for all variants in Table 7 and Table I.1.

old: The default configuration is β=0.5, Bmax=64, nmin=32, δ=0.05, and smin=2. Each sensitivity row changes only the named parameter. Here, smin counts votes remaining after exclusion of the current node. Setting β=0 retains the empirical local distribution without extra majority-class sharpening. Random grouping preserves the default group sizes; raw X and A2X change the representation used for grouping, as described in Section 4.3.3.
new: The default values are β=0.5, Bmax=64, nmin=32, δ=0.05, and smin=2. Each sensitivity row changes only the indicated parameter. The voting threshold smin applies after the current node is excluded. Setting β=0 removes the extra weight on the most-voted class but retains the empirical local distribution. Random grouping preserves the default ball sizes; raw X and A2X replace the representation used for grouping, as described in Section 4.3.3.

old: When two configurations produced exactly the same target tensor for a given dataset and seed, they shared the same training result. Thus, the 270 configuration–dataset–seed combinations required 214 training runs and 56 exact-target reuses. Equality of the targets was checked directly; the reused entries are not additional independent observations.
new: Configurations with identical target tensors for the same dataset and seed shared one training result. The 270 evaluated combinations therefore comprise 214 training runs and 56 reuses after exact target equality was verified.

old: The effect of the ball budget depends on whether it limits the partition. Cora formed 52–53 balls with both budgets of 64 and 128. CiteSeer formed 63–64 and 63–66 balls, respectively. CoraFull reached the budget in both cases: increasing it to 128 raised accuracy on all five seeds, with a paired gain of 1.57 ± 0.54 percentage points, and reduced mean target Brier score from 0.6321 to 0.6026. This is consistent with the benefit of finer regions on that dataset.
new: A larger ball budget helps only if it permits further splitting. Cora formed 52–53 balls with either budget, so increasing Bmax from 64 to 128 left its targets unchanged. CiteSeer formed 63–64 and 63–66 balls, respectively. CoraFull reached both budgets: using 128 balls improved accuracy on all five seeds, with a paired gain of 1.57 ± 0.54 percentage points, and lowered the mean target Brier score from 0.6321 to 0.6026. Finer groups were therefore beneficial on CoraFull in this comparison.

old: Increasing β to 1 improved CiteSeer on all five seeds, by 1.74 ± 0.53 points in paired differences, but the mean changes on Cora and CoraFull were only +0.04 and −0.14 points. Reducing nmin to 1 changed their means by −1.65, +0.70, and −0.05 points, respectively. Neither adjustment gives a uniform gain across the three datasets.
new: The effects of majority-class weighting and minimum ball size differed across datasets. With β=1, CiteSeer improved on all five seeds, by 1.74 ± 0.53 points in paired differences, while the mean changes on Cora and CoraFull were +0.04 and −0.14 points. Reducing nmin to 1 changed accuracy by −1.65, +0.70, and −0.05 points on Cora, CiteSeer, and CoraFull, respectively. Neither change improved all three datasets.

old: A high support requirement reduces the coverage of consensus correction. With smin=10, coverage was 56.53%, 58.32%, and 99.13% on Cora, CiteSeer, and CoraFull, respectively; the corresponding accuracy changes were −7.27, −5.22, and −0.10 points. A stricter split threshold, δ=0.10, left all nodes in one ball on every seed. Its targets were identical to those obtained from raw X and A2X. At δ=0.01, the targets instead matched the default δ=0.05 in all 15 runs. The full results distinguish stable settings from settings that prevent local regions from forming.
new: Raising the voting threshold leaves more nodes with their observed labels as targets. At smin=10, the fractions of training nodes with a positive consensus weight were 56.53%, 58.32%, and 99.13% on Cora, CiteSeer, and CoraFull, respectively. Accuracy changed by −7.27, −5.22, and −0.10 points. The larger losses on Cora and CiteSeer accompanied the lower coverage of consensus supervision. A stricter split threshold, δ=0.10, prevented splitting on every seed and produced the same single-ball targets as raw X and A2X. In contrast, δ=0.01 gave the same targets as the default δ=0.05 in all 15 runs.

old: Table I.2 evaluates the decomposition in Eq. (H.5) on the default runs. For each seed, the reduction on corrupted labels is the sum of their one-hot errors minus their soft-target errors, divided by the total number of training nodes. The cost on correct labels is the sum of their soft-target errors, divided by the same denominator; their original one-hot error is zero. The net reduction is the former minus the latter. We then average each quantity over five seeds. Clean training labels are used only for these measurements.
new: Equation (H.5) separates the change in target error into two parts: the reduction on corrupted labels and the increase on initially correct labels. Table I.2 reports both for the default configuration. For each seed, each part is summed over the corresponding nodes and divided by the total number of training nodes, so their difference gives the net reduction in Brier score. The table averages these quantities over five seeds. Clean training labels are used only to evaluate target error and the local class counts examined below.

old: The reduction on corrupted labels exceeds the cost on correct labels in every dataset–seed run. The positive net values therefore reflect a balance of these two effects, rather than preservation of every correct annotation. Random grouping also reduces Brier scores relative to observed one-hot labels, yet its classification accuracy remains much lower than that of the default regions (Table I.1). Lower target error alone is therefore insufficient to explain the benefit of informative group membership.
new: In all 15 runs, the reduction on corrupted labels outweighed the increase on correct labels. The targets therefore had lower aggregate error even though some initially correct annotations were perturbed. Random grouping also lowered Brier scores, but its classification accuracy was much lower than that of GB-LCSS (Table I.1). This comparison shows why lower target error alone does not explain the benefit of grouping related nodes.

old: The positive-margin condition in Proposition 1 holds for 75.64%, 65.02%, and 36.13% of training nodes on Cora, CiteSeer, and CoraFull, respectively, when measured from the clean labels of the other training nodes in each ball and averaged across seeds. These are empirical node fractions, not estimates of the probability bound. They show why the condition must be stated explicitly: a ball can provide useful evidence for some members without its clean majority matching every member’s class.
new: We also examined the local-class condition in Proposition 1. Using clean labels for this diagnostic, we counted training nodes whose true class had more votes than any other class among the other training nodes in their ball. Averaged over seeds, these fractions were 75.64%, 65.02%, and 36.13% on Cora, CiteSeer, and CoraFull, respectively. The condition is node-specific: a dominant class within a ball can provide useful evidence for members of that class while disagreeing with other members.
